sections.h2: Marion County and its layers of government
sections.html:
Central Indiana's Marion County is home to Indianapolis, which serves as county seat and state capital alike. In 1970 a plan called Unigov combined city and county government. Beech Grove, Lawrence, Southport and the town of Speedway opted out and stayed separate. A few small included towns, among them Clermont, Homecroft and Williams Creek, keep limited local authority, and school and fire districts were never merged into the consolidated government.

The map is a three by three grid of nine townships: Pike, Washington and Lawrence on top, Wayne, Center and Warren in the middle, Decatur, Perry and Franklin below. Your township, school district and municipality together determine the levies on your bill, which is why neighbors a few miles apart can pay quite different amounts.

A typical house in the county went up in 1972, so roofs, furnaces and sewer lines are coming due for replacement. Owners facing that bill often choose to sell the house as it stands.

sections.h2: What sets a Marion County property tax bill
sections.html:
There is no one flat rate. Your parcel belongs to a taxing district, and that district's rate gets applied to assessed value once deductions and credits come off. A "Review Tax Rates" page on indy.gov, run by the Treasurer, shows the rate for any year.

Three county offices each own a piece of the bill:

  • The Assessor decides assessed values and hears appeals.
  • The Auditor processes the homestead, mortgage and other deductions; the Recorder's deed page sends owners here.
  • The Treasurer mails the bill, collects payment and passes the money to the taxing bodies.

Homestead rules changed under a 2025 state law. For the 2026 assessment date the standard deduction falls to $40,000 from $48,000, then loses another $10,000 each year until it disappears with the 2030 assessment date. Meanwhile the supplemental deduction percentage climbs, reaching 46 percent for taxes payable in 2027, and a new supplemental homestead credit worth 10 percent of the bill, capped at $300, begins in 2026.

Sellers feel this less than buyers do. Whoever buys your house must apply for their own homestead deduction after closing, so their first bill may not look like yours.

sections.h2: Offices, due dates and ways to pay
sections.html:
Two installments a year, spring and fall, with the fall one due November 10. The Treasurer's Office in the City-County Building takes the payments.

You have five ways to pay: online, phone, mail, a bank, or at the counter. Logging in to an account lets you set up recurring payments and switch to paperless statements. Around a due date, look at the Treasurer's page first for holiday closings and extended hours.

sections.h2: Late penalties and the tax sale
sections.html:
A payment made within 30 days of the deadline, on a parcel with no earlier balance, carries a 5 percent penalty. Let that window close with tax and penalty unpaid and the rate rises to 10 percent.

Long-delinquent parcels can end up at a tax sale. The county attaches a lien to a home with unpaid taxes and auctions the lien online in the fall. An owner who wants the parcel pulled must clear everything owed before that year's cutoff: taxes, penalties, special assessments, solid waste and stormwater fees, plus a $325 administration fee. Acceptable payment is cash, a certified check, a cashier's check or a money order. Personal and business checks are refused.

A payment plan, partial payments and paying after a sale each have their own page on the Treasurer's site. Call (317) 327-4444 and ask which one fits your parcel.

Your appeal is a written Form 130 sent to the Assessor. The June 15 deadline lands in the year the bill is mailed if the notice of assessment went out after May 1, and in the assessment year if it went out earlier.

An informal meeting with the Assessor comes next. When it settles nothing, the Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals has 180 days from the petition to hold a hearing. After that the road leads to the Indiana Board of Tax Review via Form 131.

While the appeal is open you may pay on last year's assessment with no penalty, under Indiana Code 6-1.1-15-10. Attach a short written explanation for the Treasurer. If you lose, the difference is still due.

Owners hurt by recent flooding can ask for a review by submitting Form 137R, and the Assessor also lists a disaster reassessment petition among its services.

sections.h2: Taxes when you sell a Marion County house
sections.html:
You owe the tax for the stretch you owned the house, and the title company normally settles it at closing. Because Indiana bills in arrears, an installment may still be open the day you close.

Before listing or accepting an offer, collect:

  • Your latest tax statement and parcel number.
  • Proof that the last installment was paid, or the amount still owed.
  • Any pending Form 130 appeal, since it changes what the bill should be.
  • Confirmation from the Treasurer that the parcel is not on the tax sale list.

Transfer paperwork starts at the Assessor. Room W121 stamps deeds and sales disclosures, charging $10 per parcel and $20 per disclosure form, and the stamped deed moves on to the Recorder at $35 per document. The disclosure form itself is built in the Properly online system.

Timing works like this. Ask the Treasurer for the current balance, send it to the title company, and let the title company build the payoff into the closing statement. After closing, the deed goes through the Assessor stamp and the Recorder, and the buyer files for any deductions through the Auditor. Keep copies of every receipt until the closing is done, since they settle a dispute faster than a phone call does.

If the house needs work, a cash sale means you hand over the keys without hiring a contractor, scheduling inspections or answering repair requests. You pick the closing date with the title company, and the offer accounts for the condition. Compare that with the cost of repairs and months of carrying taxes on a house that is not selling.

Back taxes, a lien or an unfinished estate make a house hard to sell on the open market. Selling as-is lets the unpaid balance come out of the price rather than out of your pocket beforehand, and a cash buyer has no lender appraisal or repair list to wait on.

faqs.q: When is Marion County property tax due?
faqs.a: Two installments, spring and fall. The fall one is due November 10, and the Treasurer's page has the spring date and any holiday closings.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Marion County property tax in person?
faqs.a: Visit the Treasurer in the City-County Building, Suite 1001. Regular hours run weekdays from 8 AM to 4:30 PM, and (317) 327-4444 reaches the office.

faqs.q: How late can I file a Marion County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: June 15, either in the assessment year or in the year the bill is mailed, depending on when your notice went out. The Assessor at (317) 327-4907 can tell you which.

faqs.q: Can I stop a Marion County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, if you act before the sale by paying everything owed plus the $325 administration fee ahead of the Treasurer's cutoff. After a sale, call the Treasurer to learn your options.

faqs.q: Who stamps a deed in Marion County before it is recorded?
faqs.a: The Assessor, at Room W121. Only then does the deed go to the Recorder. The Assessor's fees are $10 per parcel and $20 for a sales disclosure when required.
